Since 6.2 each that has either hook sets it to false, and `BaseHandler.load_middleware` runs them synchronously: together they make one call into the request's thread, and the centre of the chain one call back to the loop (`django/middleware/common.py:CommonMiddleware.async_capable`, `django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.load_middleware`).

The release notes give the repeated switching as the reason, and allow that a deployment with much concurrent I/O outside the ORM may prefer it to a thread held for each request (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`).

The mixin's own flag is still true (`django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin`), so a project's middleware built on it can still run asynchronously, and a subclass of Django's that sets the flag back can run in async mode again.

`RemoteUserMiddleware`, not built on the mixin, declares both flags; `LoginRequiredMiddleware` and `XViewMiddleware` have neither hook and keep the mixin's (`django/contrib/auth/middleware.py:RemoteUserMiddleware`).

The old module answers the old import through its module-level `__getattr__`, which warns with `RemovedInDjango2029Warning` and returns the same class (`django/utils/deprecation.py:__getattr__`; [What still warns: the deprecations and the releases that end them](deprecations.md)).

Since 6.2 it passes `thread_sensitive=True`, so the error view runs on the request's own thread, where before it ran on a shared pool (`django/core/handlers/exception.py:convert_exception_to_response`).

The release notes' reason is the database: a connection belongs to the thread that opened it, and the change lets `close_old_connections`, which runs on the request's thread as the request starts and ends, manage the connections a `handler404` or a `handler500` uses (`django/db/utils.py:ConnectionHandler.thread_critical`, `django/db/__init__.py:close_old_connections`).

Since 5.0 an `"http.disconnect"` that comes before the response is made is handled, so that a view can clean up (`docs/releases/5.0.txt`).

A disconnect cancels the work: a coroutine view is cancelled where it awaits, and can clean up, while synchronous code already running in the request's thread runs to its end (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.handle`; [The two entry points](../handlers/entry.md#an-asgi-request)).

Since 6.0 the several `"cookie"` headers that HTTP/2 allows are joined with a semicolon and a space into one `"HTTP_COOKIE"`, where any other repeated header is joined with commas (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIRequest.__init__`; [Making the request: `WSGIRequest` and `ASGIRequest`](../http/request.md)).
The view decorators did not support coroutine views before 5.0 (`docs/releases/5.0.txt`).

Since then each decorator of `django/views/decorators/` but `sensitive_variables`, and each made from a middleware, picks when it is applied a `def` wrapper or an `async def` one that awaits the view (`django/views/decorators/http.py:require_http_methods`, `django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`); since 5.2 `method_decorator` marks its replacement as a coroutine function when the method is one (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`).

`sensitive_variables` takes a coroutine by not wrapping it: it records the names under the function's file and first line, where the error reporter looks (`django/views/decorators/debug.py:sensitive_variables`).

Passing it any value but `None` warns with `RemovedInDjango2029Warning`, and `safe=True` still raises `TypeError` for a value that is not a dictionary (`django/http/response.py:JsonResponse.__init__`; [The response object](../http/response.md#jsonresponse)).

Since 6.1 `MultiPartParser.parse` decodes a part sent with a `"base64"` transfer encoding through `base64.b64decode` with `validate=True`, so a character outside the Base64 alphabet makes the data invalid (in a file, white space is removed first); before, the notes say, invalid data could be silently ignored or give empty values (`django/http/multipartparser.py:MultiPartParser.parse`; [Multipart parsing and upload handlers](../http/uploads.md)).
